title: The Candle
text:
On an estate in the days of serfdom, the owner hired a steward named Michael Semyonovich who treated the peasants with relentless cruelty. He worked them without rest, fined them, and had them flogged for the smallest fault. The peasants hated him and began talking among themselves about killing him.

Then he ordered them to plow his fields on Easter Sunday, the greatest holy day of the year. The peasants were furious, and the talk of murder grew louder. One man, Peter Mikhyeev, refused to join in. Killing a man, he said, was a far worse sin than working on a holy day, and the evil would fall on whoever did it.

On Easter Peter went out to plow as ordered. He fixed a lighted wax candle to his plow, the kind lit in church at Easter, and plowed singing the Easter hymn. All day the candle never went out.

When the steward heard about it, he was shaken. He went pale and said that Peter had beaten him. Soon afterward he fell from his horse and was killed. The peasants were freed from him without having to take his life.
lesson: Cruelty from those in charge invites hatred and revenge. One person's quiet refusal to answer evil with evil can do more to break that cycle than violence.
people: Michael Semyonovich the steward, Peter Mikhyeev
